title: Good cellular trees for a weakly saturated class
statement:
Fix a universe $\mathcal U$; small means $\mathcal U$-small, and colimits mean [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. A cardinal $\tau$ is regular if unions of fewer than $\tau$ sets of size less than $\tau$ have size less than $\tau$. A category is $\tau$-filtered if each diagram with fewer than $\tau$ morphisms admits a cocone. An object is $\tau$-presentable if its Hom functor preserves small $\tau$-filtered colimits. Let $\tau\in\mathcal U$ be uncountable regular and let $\mathcal A$ have small Hom sets, all small colimits, and a small family of $\tau$-presentable objects under whose small $\tau$-filtered colimits every object is obtained. A weakly saturated arrow class contains all isomorphisms and is closed under pushouts, small continuous transfinite compositions, and retracts in the arrow category (arrows are objects, commuting squares are morphisms; a retract of $g$ is an $f$ with maps $s:f\to g$, $r:g\to f$ and $rs=1_f$). A pushout is a colimit of a span. Continuous means that at each nonzero limit ordinal the object is the colimit of its predecessors. Let $C$ be weakly saturated, and let $K$ be the class of its arrows with $\tau$-presentable source and target. Suppose $C$ is the weakly saturated closure of a small subset of $K$.

For any arrow class $L$, an $L$-tree with root $X$ consists of a small well-founded poset $T$ (each nonempty subset has a minimal element), a diagram $t\mapsto(X\to Y_t)$ in the undercategory $X/\mathcal A$ (its objects are maps out of $X$, and its morphisms are commuting triangles), and, for every $t$, a map $P_t\to Q_t$ in $L$ and an attaching map $P_t\to Y_{<t}$ such that the canonical map $Y_{<t}\to Y_t$ induced by the diagram is a pushout of $P_t\to Q_t$ along the attaching map: there is a map $Q_t\to Y_t$ making the square commute, and the square is a pushout, so $Y_t\cong Y_{<t}\amalg_{P_t}Q_t$ by an isomorphism under $Y_{<t}$. Here $Y_{<t}$ is the colimit of the predecessor diagram in $X/\mathcal A$; an empty colimit in that undercategory is $X$. For downward-closed $E\subseteq T$ write $Y_E$ for the restricted colimit in $X/\mathcal A$, so $Y_\varnothing=X$. Such a tree is $\tau$-good if $P_t,Q_t$ are $\tau$-presentable and each predecessor set has cardinality less than $\tau$.

Every $f:X\to Y$ in $C$ admits a $\tau$-good $K$-tree with $X\to Y_T$ isomorphic to $f$ in $X/\mathcal A$. For every $L$-tree and downward-closed $E\subseteq F\subseteq T$, the map $Y_E\to Y_F$ belongs to the weakly saturated closure of $L$. If the tree is $\tau$-good, this map is itself the colimit map of a $\tau$-good $L$-tree with root $Y_E$ and indexing poset $F\setminus E$, with the inherited order.

source.place: Definition A.1.5.1 and Notation A.1.5.2 (printed pp. 799-800), Remark A.1.5.5 and Lemma A.1.5.6 (pp. 800-801), Proposition A.1.5.12 and Corollary A.1.5.13 (pp. 808-809). Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this cellular-tree result.

proof.text: First establish the colimit calculus used throughout. For downward-closed $E,F\subseteq T$, the square $Y_{E\cap F}\to Y_E$, $Y_F\to Y_{E\cup F}$ is a pushout: a map from its proposed apex is exactly a pair of cocones under $X$ on $E,F$ agreeing on their overlap. The assertion holds when any subset is empty, with $Y_\varnothing=X$. A union of an increasing chain of downward-closed subsets has colimit the colimit of their $Y$-objects, by the same cocone test. For $E\subseteq F$, define, for $t\in F\setminus E$, $Z_t=Y_{E\cup\{s\in F:s\le t\}}$. Its predecessor colimit under $Y_E$ is $Y_{E\cup\{s:s<t\}}$, since all $s<t$ lie in $F$. The union pushout square identifies its map to $Z_t$ as a pushout of the original cell $P_t\to Q_t$. Its total colimit is $Y_F$. This constructs the required relative tree with inherited order and the same cells, and preserves goodness because its predecessor sets are subsets of the original ones.

source.place: Notation A.1.5.2 and Remarks A.1.5.3, A.1.5.5; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: For an arbitrary $L$-tree, well-order its small indexing set and recursively select the first minimal element of the remaining poset. Each earlier set is downward-closed. This procedure exhausts the set at a small ordinal: otherwise its distinct selections would inject an ordinal of cardinality greater than the set into the set. Write $E_\alpha$ for the selected initial sets, with unions at limits. The successor $Y_{E_\alpha}\to Y_{E_{\alpha+1}}$ is the pushout of the cell at the selected element: first use its defining square and then the union pushout of Step 1. The chain is continuous by Step 1, so its map from $X$ to $Y_T$ belongs to the weakly saturated closure of $L$. Apply this argument to the relative tree of Step 1 to obtain the transition clause for all $E\subseteq F$. An empty tree gives the identity, which is in that closure.

source.place: Lemma A.1.5.6, with the minimal-element enumeration made explicit; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: We will use the following thinning construction, proved here for any tree with $\tau$-presentable cells. Process its elements in the minimal-element enumeration of Step 2. Maintain a weaker partial order $\preceq$ (so $s\preceq t$ implies $s\le t$), a good tree on the processed elements, and comparison maps to the old objects inducing an isomorphism of colimits on every old downward-closed subset. At limits take unions of the constructed orders and diagrams; their comparison remains an isomorphism by the cocone criterion. At a new element $t$, its old predecessor subset $B$ has already been processed. In the new order, the downward-closed subsets $D\subseteq B$ of size less than $\tau$ form a small $\tau$-filtered poset: the downward closure of fewer than $\tau$ elements still has size less than $\tau$, by regularity and the inductively small predecessor sets, and a union of fewer than $\tau$ such subsets is an upper bound. Their $Y'_D$ have colimit $Y'_B$, since compatible cocones on all these subsets are exactly cocones on $B$. Filtered colimits under $X$ have the same underlying colimit in $\mathcal A$: the nonempty filtered indexing category makes all its maps from $X$ agree. Presentability of $P_t$ and the elementwise filtered-colimit statement therefore factor $P_t\to Y_B\cong Y'_B$ through some $Y'_D$. Give $t$ precisely the elements of $D$ as strict predecessors and set $Y'_t=Y'_D\amalg_{P_t}Q_t$. The resulting map $Y'_t\to Y_t$ comes from the old square. If an old downward-closed subset contains $t$, its new colimit is its earlier new colimit pushed out along $P_t\to Q_t$: this follows from the defining pushout and its cocone maps. Induction thus identifies it with the old colimit. All predecessor sets stay small, the new order is well-founded as a subrelation of the old order, and the final colimit under $X$ is unchanged. This proves thinning, including for the empty tree, without treating it as a black-box existence lemma.

source.place: Lemma A.1.5.7, construction and comparison invariant; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: For compact-root descent of a tree with fewer than $\tau$ cells, write its arbitrary root $V$ as a small $\tau$-filtered colimit of $\tau$-presentable $V_i$. The filtered-poset reindexing lemma makes the index a small $\tau$-filtered poset $I$. Choose $i\in I$ (the empty subset has an upper bound), and take the empty descended tree over $V_i$. Apply partial cellular root descent extension with $E=\varnothing$. Its hypotheses hold because all cell sources are $\tau$-presentable. It gives $j\ge i$ and a tree with root $M=V_j$ on the same poset and with the same cells, whose specified objectwise pushout to $V$ is the original tree. The small-tree presentability lemma gives a $\tau$-presentable total object $N$, since $M$ and both endpoints of every cell are presentable and there are fewer than $\tau$ cells. Put $h:M\to N$. Maps out of $N\amalg_M V$ are exactly cocones under $V$ on the base-changed tree, so its total arrow is the pushout of $h$. Step 2 puts $h$ in the weakly saturated closure of the cells. No presentability of $V$ is used.

source.place: Lemma A.1.5.11; explicit compact-root descent for use below; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: Choose the small subset $I\subseteq K$ whose weak saturation is $C$, and put $R=I^{\square}$. The left lifting class ${}^{\square}R$ contains $I$ and all isomorphisms (use the inverse for a filler). Its pushout and retract closure follow from the lifting-class lemma and its transfinite closure from the transfinite lifting lemma. Hence $C\subseteq{}^{\square}R$. Apply the cellular small-object factorization to $f:X\to Y$, obtaining $X\xrightarrow{j}V\xrightarrow{p}Y$ with $p\in R$ and $j$ a small continuous composite of pushouts of small coproducts of members of $I$. The square with sides $f,p$ and horizontal maps $j,1_Y$ has a lift $s:Y\to V$ with $sf=j$ and $ps=1_Y$. Thus $Y$ is a retract of $V$ under $X$. To obtain an ordinary $I$-tree for $j$, well-order the cells of each coproduct and attach them one at a time; a cocone on these successive pushouts is precisely a map from the old object together with maps from all the target summands agreeing on their source summands, which is the original coproduct pushout. At limits the same cocone test identifies colimits. Lexicographically concatenating these small well-orders gives a small well-ordered $I$-tree with total $V$.

source.place: Remark A.1.2.8 and the beginning of the proof of Proposition A.1.5.12; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: Thin the tree of Step 5 by Step 3. Its cells lie in $I\subseteq K$, so their endpoints are $\tau$-presentable. Denote the resulting good tree by $(Y_t)_{t\in T}$ with root $X$, and identify $Y_T$ with $V$. The endomorphism $e_T=sp$ of $Y_T$ is idempotent under $X$ and its specified retract image is $Y$. We will resolve this idempotent along small blocks rather than claim that a retract of a good tree is automatically a good tree.

source.place: Proposition A.1.5.12, after applying Lemma A.1.5.7; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: An idempotent $e:A\to A$ splits using a coequalizer $q:A\to Z$ of $e,1_A$: since $e$ equalizes them, there is a unique $j:Z\to A$ with $jq=e$, and $qj=1_Z$ follows after precomposition with the epimorphism $q$. If $u:A\to A'$ commutes with idempotents, its induced image map is $q'uj$, and these maps preserve identities and composition. Thus a compatible diagram of idempotents has an image diagram and is a retract of the original diagram. Colimits commute with these images: a map out of an image is a map $v$ out of the original object with $ve=v$, and the colimit universal property identifies such maps with compatible families having that equality. This also works under $X$ when the idempotents fix its structural maps, with image of $1_X$ equal to $X$. Further, compatible endomorphisms on $Y_E,Y_F$ agreeing on $Y_{E\cap F}$ amalgamate uniquely to an endomorphism on $Y_{E\cup F}$ by Step 1; if they are idempotents, the amalgamation is idempotent by uniqueness.

source.place: Image and amalgamation operations implicit in Proposition A.1.5.12, written from colimit universal properties; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: Construct a continuous increasing exhaustion $B_\alpha$ of $T$ and idempotents $e_\alpha$ on $Y_{B_\alpha}$ compatible with one another and with $e_T$. Set $B_0=\varnothing$ and $e_0=1_X$. At a limit take the union and colimit idempotent, using Step 1. If $B_\alpha\ne T$, choose a minimal $t\in T\setminus B_\alpha$ and apply the compatible-idempotent enlargement lemma to $B=B_\alpha$ and $E_0=\{t\}$. It gives a downward-closed $D_\alpha$ of size less than $\tau$ with idempotents on $Y_{D_\alpha}$ and $Y_{B_\alpha\cap D_\alpha}$, compatible with $e_\alpha$ and $e_T$. Set $B_{\alpha+1}=B_\alpha\cup D_\alpha$ and amalgamate its idempotent by Step 7. The three commutation equalities in that lemma give exactly the two restrictions required for the amalgamation and its compatibility with $e_T$. Each successor adds the selected new element; the recursion therefore terminates at a small ordinal $\theta$ with $B_\theta=T$, by the distinct-element bound of Step 2. Compatibility with $e_T$ then implies $e_\theta=e_T$.

source.place: Proposition A.1.5.12, compatible small-block exhaustion using Lemma A.1.5.9; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: Fix $\alpha<\theta$, write $B=B_\alpha$, $D=D_\alpha$, and $H=B\cap D$. By Step 1 the relative map $Y_H\to Y_D$ is a tree on $D\setminus B$, with fewer than $\tau$ cells, all in $K$. Step 4 supplies a pushout presentation by a map $h:M\to N$ with presentable endpoints and $h\in\operatorname{wsat}(K)\subseteq C$. The union square of Step 1 exhibits $Y_B\to Y_{B\cup D}$ as its further pushout, hence as a pushout of $h$. Splitting the compatible idempotents as in Step 7 gives an image arrow $Z_\alpha\to Z_{\alpha+1}$ which is an arrow retract of this map. Apply compact pushout retract descent to $u=h$. It produces a map $k_\alpha:M_\alpha\to N_\alpha$ with presentable endpoints whose pushout is $Z_\alpha\to Z_{\alpha+1}$ and with $k_\alpha\in\operatorname{wsat}(\{h\})\subseteq C$. Consequently $k_\alpha\in K$. Here $\operatorname{wsat}(K)\subseteq C$ and $\operatorname{wsat}(\{h\})\subseteq C$ follow directly from $K\subseteq C$, $h\in C$, and weak saturation of $C$; they do not require an assumption on the root or on the image objects.

source.place: Proposition A.1.5.12, successor maps; Lemmas A.1.5.10-11; reconstructed argument, online source not archived

proof.text: Choose $Z_\alpha$ functorially as the images in Step 7. Their diagram starts at $Z_0=X$ and is continuous, because $Y_{B_\alpha}$ and the idempotents are continuous at limits and Step 7 identifies the colimit of the images with the image of the colimit. Its final object $Z_\theta$ is isomorphic to the given retract $Y$ under $X$: if $q:V\to Z_\theta$, $j:Z_\theta\to V$ split $sp$, the maps $qs:Y\to Z_\theta$ and $pj:Z_\theta\to Y$ are inverse, using $ps=1$, $jq=sp$ and $qj=1$. Each successor is a pushout of $k_\alpha\in K$ by Step 9. The well-ordered tree with cells indexed by $\alpha<\theta$, object $Z_{\alpha+1}$ at $\alpha$, and root $X$ has predecessor colimit $Z_\alpha$ and total $Y$. Thin it by Step 3 to obtain a $\tau$-good $K$-tree. When $\theta=0$ take the empty tree. Steps 1-2 already prove both the relative-good-tree and weak-saturation transition clauses, completing every assertion.

source.place: Corollary A.1.5.13 and conclusion of Proposition A.1.5.12; reconstructed argument, online source not archived
